broad.question: For high-entropy alloys intended for aerospace fasteners, what single intervention could improve the combination of mechanical durability, room-temperature creep resistance, and corrosion resistance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an untreated baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence that supports it, and an experiment with clear results that would falsify it.

hypotheses.label: C1

source_paper.title: Effect of serrated grain boundary on tensile and creep properties of a precipitation strengthened high entropy alloy.

hypotheses.builds_on: the established concept in superalloy literature that trace additions of reactive elements (e.g., Y) segregate to grain boundaries to improve interfacial cohesion and oxidation resistance.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This approach proposes a minor compositional modification as a single intervention to achieve simultaneous improvements in room-temperature mechanical properties, creep resistance, and corrosion behavior in HEAs used for aerospace fasteners—a route not explored in the original paper.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Slightly modify the alloy composition by adding a controlled trace amount of a grain boundary segregant (e.g., yttrium) to enhance grain boundary cohesion and promote the formation of protective oxides, thus improving mechanical durability, room-temperature creep resistance, and corrosion resistance.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: SLM‐fabricated HEA with a baseline composition currently containing minor elements including B (0.01 wt.%) but without intentional additions of reactive rare-earth elements.
hypothesis.intervention: Introduce an additional trace element, such as 0.05 wt.% yttrium, into the prealloyed powder prior to gas atomization or by surface coating and subsequent diffusion treatment. This addition is designed to segregate to the grain boundaries during subsequent processing and heat treatment.
hypothesis.conditions: The modified alloy processing follows the same solution treatment (≥1120°C) and heat treatment schedule as the baseline HEA, ensuring that during cooling and aging, Y atoms preferentially segregate to the grain boundaries. The addition is low enough not to disturb the overall phase equilibria yet sufficient to influence interfacial chemistry. This intervention is intended for HEAs used in aerospace fasteners operating at room temperature.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: Enhanced grain boundary cohesion and stability due to yttrium segregation at the boundaries, plus the promotion of a more adherent and protective oxide layer at the boundaries.
hypothesis.mechanism: Yttrium is known in superalloys to segregate to grain boundaries where it improves cohesion and retards the initiation and propagation of intergranular cracks. It can also lead to the formation of a finely adherent Y-rich oxide during exposure to oxidizing environments, which stabilizes the passive film. Together, these effects can reduce creep deformation at room temperature by limiting dislocation motion along weak interfaces and improve corrosion resistance by minimizing localized corrosion attack at the grain boundaries.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Compared with the baseline HEA, the yttrium-doped alloy is expected to exhibit enhanced mechanical durability (e.g., a measurable reduction in propagation of intergranular cracks under cyclic loading), lower room-temperature creep strain under sustained load (improved by a quantifiable margin, tentatively on the order of 20%), and improved corrosion metrics (such as lower corrosion current densities from electrochemical tests).
hypothesis.baseline: HEA processed with the original composition and standard heat treatment without any intentional grain boundary segregant addition.
hypothesis.boundary: The improvement is sensitive to the precise Y content; too little may have no effect, whereas too much might lead to the formation of unwanted Y-rich phases that could embrittle the alloy. Control over Y distribution is critical.
hypothesis.uncertainty: While grain boundary segregation of reactive elements like Y is well-established in nickel-based superalloys, direct quantitative correlation in HEAs at room temperature is less documented, so the exact magnitude of the improvements remains to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of HEA specimens: one with the standard composition and one with an additional 0.05 wt.% Y. Ensure identical SLM fabrication and heat treatments. Use atom probe tomography or TEM-EDS to verify Y segregation at grain boundaries. Then, perform room-temperature creep tests, fatigue/durability assessments, and corrosion tests (e.g., potentiodynamic polarization) to compare the performance.
measurements: Quantification of Y segregation at grain boundaries via microanalysis
Room-temperature creep strain and fatigue life measurements
Corrosion parameters such as corrosion current density and passivation behavior
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the yttrium-enhanced specimens do not show a statistically significant improvement (for example, >20% gain in durability or creep resistance and improved corrosion metrics) relative to the baseline, or if deleterious secondary phases form, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C10

source_paper.title: New HfNbTaTiZr High-Entropy Alloy Coatings Produced by Electrospark Deposition with High Corrosion Resistance.

hypotheses.builds_on: the established high corrosion resistance of electrospark deposited HfNbTaTiZr HEA coatings (PMC8348113) and leverages known alumina-passivation benefits from studies on nickel aluminide and superalloys.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces a compositional adjustment (Al addition) with explicit prior thermodynamic calibration to ensure phase stability, targeting a simultaneous enhancement in corrosion protection, mechanical durability, and creep resistance in an aerospace fastener application.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Introducing a minor 3–5 at.% Al addition into the HfNbTaTiZr HEA, with prior thermodynamic calibration to ensure BCC phase stability, to promote the in situ formation of a thin, adherent alumina (Al2O3) passivation layer without destabilizing the structure.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: The base material is an equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr HEA processed via mechanical alloying, spark plasma sintering, and electrospark deposition, exhibiting a predominantly BCC structure with high corrosion resistance and good mechanical properties.
hypothesis.intervention: Modify the alloy composition to include 3–5 at.% Al by pre-mixing the appropriate elemental powders followed by the same processing route (mechanical alloying, SPS consolidation, and electrospark deposition). Prior to full-scale processing, use thermodynamic modeling and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to confirm that the added Al will not destabilize the BCC phase.
hypothesis.conditions: Maintain the conventional processing parameters in an inert (argon) atmosphere throughout alloying and coating deposition. Verify the composition and phase stability at ambient temperature as found in aerospace fastener operational environments (room temperature with aggressive corrosive agents).
hypothesis.structural_mediator: The controlled Al addition is anticipated to segregate subtly to the surface during electrospark deposition and service, forming a continuous, nanometric Al2O3 layer while remaining in solid solution in the interior to yield solid-solution strengthening.
hypothesis.mechanism: Owing to its high oxygen affinity, Al will react with trace oxygen during service or minor post-deposition oxidation to form a stable alumina film that acts as a barrier against corrosion. Simultaneously, the dissolved Al atoms provide solid-solution strengthening, thereby reducing dislocation mobility that contributes to room-temperature creep. Thermodynamic validations ensure that the desired BCC structure is preserved without forming brittle intermetallics.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated HEA, the Al-modified HEA should display lower corrosion current density (icorr) due to an effective passivation layer, improved surface hardness, and a modest reduction in creep strain rate. The expected improvements are moderate but statistically significant, pending quantitative experimental validation.
hypothesis.baseline: Untreated HfNbTaTiZr HEA produced via the described processing route, as characterized in PMC8348113.
hypothesis.boundary: The beneficial effects depend on maintaining a low Al content; exceeding ~5 at.% could induce unwanted phase transformations or embrittlement. The preliminary thermodynamic analysis and DSC tests are essential to determine the safe compositional window.
hypothesis.uncertainty: Uncertainty remains regarding the precise segregation behavior of Al during rapid cooling and whether the alumina layer will form uniformly without compromising the overall BCC stability. Quantitative improvement magnitudes require experimental confirmation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sample sets: one using standard HfNbTaTiZr and one with an added 3–5 at.% Al. Validate phase stability via XRD and DSC. Process both via identical mechanical alloying, SPS, and electrospark deposition. Subject them to standardized corrosion tests in 3.5% NaCl solution and room-temperature creep tests under fixed load.
measurements: XRD and DSC for phase confirmation
Electrochemical measurements (Ecorr, icorr) via Tafel analysis
Microhardness and creep strain measurements under controlled load
SEM/EDS to verify the formation and continuity of the alumina layer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-modified HEA does not exhibit statistically significant improvements in corrosion resistance (lower icorr), enhanced hardness, or reduced room-temperature creep relative to the baseline—or if microstructural characterization reveals destabilization of the BCC phase—the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C13

source_paper.title: Interstitial atoms enable joint twinning and transformation induced plasticity in strong and ductile high-entropy alloys.

hypotheses.builds_on: the observed benefits of nanoscale carbide dispersion and twin-induced plasticity in the dual-phase HEA from PMC5227964, extending the strategy by introducing a heat-treatment step to further refine and stabilize the nano-constituent framework.
hypotheses.what_is_new: It proposes a novel post–cold-rolling low-temperature short-time annealing treatment to optimize the dispersion of strengthening nano-carbides, specifically targeting improvements in room-temperature creep and corrosion resistance, an intervention not discussed in the original study.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Tailored Low-Temperature Short-Time Annealing to Stabilize Nano-Precipitate Dispersion and Enhance Creep and Corrosion Performance
hypothesis.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy processed as in PMC5227964 with dual-phase microstructure comprising an f.c.c. matrix, interstitial carbon, and nano-carbide precipitates formed during standard thermomechanical processing.
hypothesis.intervention: Introduce an additional heat treatment step consisting of a very short (e.g., 1–3 minutes) annealing at a lower temperature (around 700°C) immediately after cold rolling, followed by rapid quenching.
hypothesis.conditions: The alloy is produced by the same melting and thermomechanical route as in PMC5227964, but after cold rolling the specimen is annealed at 700°C for a precisely controlled short time in an inert atmosphere (e.g., argon) to prevent oxidation, then water-quenched.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: This annealing is designed to further refine and homogenize the distribution of nano-carbides (M23C6) without promoting their coarsening, thereby maintaining a high density of obstacles (particles) within the f.c.c. matrix.
hypothesis.mechanism: At lower annealing temperatures and short times, diffusion of substitutional and interstitial atoms is limited, preventing significant growth of precipitates while relieving residual stresses and promoting a uniform dispersion of nano-carbides. The fine carbide dispersion enhances dislocation pinning (through an Orowan mechanism) and retards grain boundary sliding, thus improving room-temperature creep resistance. In addition, a uniform and refined microstructure can lead to a more homogeneous passive surface film that is less prone to localized corrosion attack.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Modest improvements (expected in the range of 10–20%) in yield and tensile strengths and a noticeable decrease in room-temperature creep strain under constant load, along with enhanced corrosion resistance (evidenced by a reduced corrosion current density) relative to the baseline processing route.
hypothesis.baseline: The standard interstitial TWIP-TRIP‑HEA processed as described in PMC5227964 without the additional low-temperature annealing step.
hypothesis.boundary: Too low a temperature or an excessively short annealing time may not sufficiently homogenize the nano-carbide dispersion, while too high a temperature or longer times could lead to carbide coarsening and loss of strengthening benefits. Thus, precise control is essential.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The optimal annealing parameters (temperature and time) need to be determined; the quantitative improvements may vary with slight deviations in the processing conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two sets of HEA specimens: one using the standard processing route (as in PMC5227964) and one with the additional low-temperature, short-time annealing. Characterize the nano-precipitate size and distribution (using TEM or APT) and perform room-temperature tensile and creep tests along with corrosion tests (potentiodynamic polarization).
measurements: Grain and precipitate size distributions
Tensile properties including yield and ultimate strength
Creep strain under a fixed constant load over time
Corrosion current density and potential
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified heat-treated samples fail to show significant improvements in nano-precipitate uniformity, mechanical durability, creep resistance, and corrosion behavior compared to the standard samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C4

source_paper.title: The High Temperature Tensile and Creep Behaviors of High Entropy Superalloy.

hypotheses.builds_on: the general principles of surface treatment improvements seen in stainless steels and superalloys as highlighted in background texts, applied to the HEA fastener context.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes a post-processing surface nitriding step as a single intervention to address both mechanical surface durability and corrosion issues in HEA fasteners—a route not explored in the paper, which focused solely on bulk microstructure and conventional heat treatments.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Apply a surface nitriding treatment to form a thin, diffusion-based nitride layer on the HEA fastener surfaces, which will enhance mechanical wear resistance, inhibit surface-initiated creep deformation at room temperature, and improve corrosion resistance.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: A high-entropy superalloy with a bulk microstructure of high entropy FCC γ matrix and coherent spherical γ′ precipitates, exhibiting satisfactory tensile properties but with potential surface vulnerabilities to corrosion and localized creep (or stress concentration effects) at room temperature.
hypothesis.intervention: Subject the final machined fastener components to a low-temperature gas nitriding process (e.g., NH3 atmosphere, around 500–550 °C for several hours) to develop a thin, hard nitride diffusion layer on the surface.
hypothesis.conditions: The nitriding process is carried out post mechanical finishing and heat-treatment, ensuring that the bulk microstructure remains unaffected. The temperature is chosen to avoid altering the interior γ/γ′ microstructure while effectively forming nitrides at the surface.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: The formation of surface nitrides (e.g., CrN or TiN) increases surface hardness and creates a compressive residual stress layer. This layer mitigates crack initiation, improves wear resistance, and forms a barrier that slows both corrosion and the onset of surface creep deformation.
hypothesis.mechanism: Nitriding introduces nitrogen diffused into the alloy surface to react with alloying elements (such as Cr, Ti) to form stable nitride phases. These phases are known to enhance surface hardness and provide excellent corrosion resistance due to reduced permeation pathways for corrosive species. The improved hardness and compressive stress field can also suppress localized dislocation activity that may cause creep-like deformation under low loads.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Sharper improvement in surface hardness and corrosion resistance, with reduced initiation of surface creep under room-temperature or cyclic loading conditions. The overall mechanical durability of aerospace fasteners is expected to increase, especially under conditions prone to wear and environmental attack.
hypothesis.baseline: Untreated HEA fasteners that have undergone standard heat treatment and machining, exhibiting the base-level corrosion resistance (via inherent Cr2O3 and Al2O3 formation) and mechanical properties reported in the paper.
hypothesis.boundary: The treatment is limited to surface layers and may not influence bulk creep properties. Excessive nitriding could lead to brittleness if the nitride layer is too thick, so the process parameters must be optimized.
hypothesis.uncertainty: While similar nitriding strategies have worked for conventional alloys, the quantitative effect on room-temperature creep in HEAs is less documented, so the magnitude of improvement is uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA fastener samples: one set receives the standard finish and the other is subjected to low-temperature gas nitriding. Conduct surface microhardness tests, wear tests, electrochemical corrosion tests (e.g., potentiodynamic polarization), and low-load creep or cyclic loading tests at room temperature. Analyze the nitrided layer thickness and phase composition using XRD and cross-sectional SEM.
measurements: Surface hardness (microhardness or nanoindentation)
Corrosion rate via electrochemical tests
Wear resistance through standard tribological tests
Observation of nitride layer thickness and phase by SEM/XRD
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nitrided samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in surface hardness, improved corrosion resistance, or reduced initiation of creep-like deformation compared to the untreated samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C5

source_paper.title: Effects of Mo Addition on Microstructure and Corrosion Resistance of Cr25-xCo25Ni25Fe25Mox High-Entropy Alloys via Directed Energy Deposition.

hypotheses.builds_on: the paper’s finding that Mo addition via DED creates a dual-phase structure (FCC + σ) which enhances strength and corrosion resistance
hypotheses.what_is_new: Integrates a controlled aging heat treatment post-DED to further refine the σ-phase microstructure, targeting room-temperature creep resistance and enhanced corrosion performance—conditions not explored in the paper.

hypothesis.hypothesis: A post-deposition aging heat treatment to refine the Mo-induced σ-phase dispersion will enhance mechanical strength, room‐temperature creep resistance, and corrosion resistance.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: DED-fabricated CrCoNiFeMo high-entropy alloy with a dual-phase (FCC + σ) microstructure as produced by powder blending with 5–10% Mo addition.
hypothesis.intervention: Apply a two-step heat treatment: first a solution treatment to homogenize the alloy followed by a short-duration aging (e.g., at ~700 °C for 1 hour) to precipitate a fine, uniformly distributed Mo-rich σ phase.
hypothesis.conditions: Heat treatment carried out in an inert atmosphere; aging parameters tuned to avoid over-coarsening, under conditions similar to precipitation hardening treatments (e.g., analogous to A286 treatment regimes) while ensuring the alloy remains in the desired dual-phase balance at room temperature.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: Uniform, nanometer-to-micrometer scale Mo-rich σ phase precipitates dispersed along grain boundaries and within grains.
hypothesis.mechanism: The fine σ-phase precipitates increase grain boundary pinning and dislocation obstruction, thereby raising yield and ultimate tensile strengths while simultaneously impeding dislocation motion responsible for room-temperature creep. Additionally, the refined microstructure reduces the number of active corrosion sites, enhancing passivation in corrosive environments such as 3.5 wt% NaCl.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-deposited alloy, an increase in yield strength (potentially in the range of an additional 10–20% improvement over the untreated state), reduced room-temperature creep under service loads, and lower corrosion current density (Icorr) in electrochemical tests.
hypothesis.baseline: As-deposited DED HEA with already improved properties from Mo alloying but without any post-processing heat treatment.
hypothesis.boundary: Excessive aging time or temperature may coarsen the σ phase too much, leading to embrittlement and degraded ductility. The intervention is optimized only within a narrow aging parameter window.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The optimal aging parameters (time and temperature) for achieving the finest σ-phase dispersion while maintaining ductility under operational conditions remain to be precisely determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of DED-fabricated Mo-containing HEA specimens: one kept in the as-deposited state (baseline) and one subjected to the proposed aging treatment. Perform standardized tensile tests, room-temperature creep tests under constant load, and potentiodynamic polarization tests in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution.
measurements: Yield and ultimate tensile strength
Creep strain over time under a fixed load
Corrosion potential (Ecorr) and corrosion current density (Icorr)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated specimens do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in strength (>=10% increase), lower creep strain rate, and improved corrosion metrics (higher Ecorr and lower Icorr) compared to the untreated baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C6

source_paper.title: Effects of Mo Addition on Microstructure and Corrosion Resistance of Cr25-xCo25Ni25Fe25Mox High-Entropy Alloys via Directed Energy Deposition.

hypotheses.builds_on: the paper’s demonstration of improved mechanical and corrosion properties with Mo addition via DED, expanded by utilizing surface stress engineering techniques common in high-performance alloys
hypotheses.what_is_new: Introduces laser shock peening—a surface treatment not explored in the paper—as a single, post-fabrication mechanical intervention to further enhance durability, creep resistance, and corrosion performance of HEA fasteners.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Application of laser shock peening (LSP) to the surface of the DED-fabricated Mo-containing HEA will improve its mechanical durability, room‐temperature creep resistance, and corrosion resistance.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: DED-manufactured high-entropy alloy fasteners containing Mo with a dual-phase FCC + σ microstructure, which may display surface tensile residual stresses and microstructural irregularities from the additive process.
hypothesis.intervention: Perform laser shock peening on the as-fabricated components using optimized laser parameters to impart deep compressive residual stresses and slightly refine the surface grain structure without altering the bulk phase composition.
hypothesis.conditions: LSP performed at ambient temperature with controlled laser energy and coverage to avoid surface over-peening; the process is applied uniformly on fastener surfaces in air or controlled atmosphere.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: A near-surface microstructure characterized by increased compressive residual stresses and a refined grain size, potentially with reduced surface defects.
hypothesis.mechanism: The compressive residual stresses induced by LSP inhibit crack initiation and retard dislocation motion, thereby reducing room-temperature creep and fatigue. Moreover, the refined surface microstructure reduces the number and size of corrosion initiation sites, leading to enhanced corrosion resistance. Collectively, these factors improve the mechanical durability of fasteners under cyclic and static loads.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated specimens, LSP-treated fasteners should exhibit higher fatigue strength, a measurable reduction in creep strain under constant load, and improved corrosion behavior (elevated Ecorr and reduced Icorr) in salt-spray or electrochemical tests.
hypothesis.baseline: As-deposited DED HEA fasteners with Mo addition, possessing the inherent dual-phase structure but without any post-fabrication surface stress modification.
hypothesis.boundary: If laser parameters are not optimized, over-peening may lead to excessive surface roughness or micro-cracking, which would negate the benefits; the effects are primarily near the surface (depth limited).
hypothesis.uncertainty: The magnitude of improvement in room-temperature creep behavior and corrosion resistance specific to this HEA, as well as the depth of beneficial compressive stress, may vary with LSP process parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA fastener specimens: one set remains untreated and the other undergoes laser shock peening. Characterize surface residual stresses (using X-ray diffraction), perform microstructural analysis (via EBSD or SEM), and conduct fatigue, creep (under constant load at room temperature), and corrosion testing (potentiodynamic polarization in NaCl solution).
measurements: Compressive residual stress magnitude and depth profile
Surface grain size and defect density
Fatigue life and creep strain measurements
Ecorr and Icorr from corrosion tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no statistically significant improvements in compressive residual stress, fatigue/creep resistance, or corrosion resistance are observed in the LSP-treated samples compared to the baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C7

source_paper.title: Investigation of the Micromechanical Behavior of a Ti68Nb7Ta3Zr4Mo18 (at.%) High-Entropy Alloy.

hypotheses.builds_on: The paper’s discussion of grain size effects, including the inverse Hall–Petch phenomenon observed for excessively fine grains, underlines the importance of microstructural control. This hypothesis uses that insight to propose a gradient grain structure that capitalizes on both fine and coarse grain benefits.
hypotheses.what_is_new: Distinct from the paper’s parameter studies, this proposal employs a single, integrated thermo-mechanical processing intervention to intentionally create a bimodal microstructure that could balance and optimize mechanical durability, creep resistance, and corrosion performance in aerospace fasteners.

hypothesis.hypothesis: A controlled thermo-mechanical processing route designed to produce a bimodal (gradient) grain size distribution in the HEA will enhance mechanical durability, improve room-temperature creep resistance, and boost corrosion resistance in aerospace fasteners.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: As-cast Ti68Nb7Ta3Zr4Mo18 HEA with a homogeneous grain structure.
hypothesis.intervention: Implement a single thermo-mechanical processing sequence consisting of cold working followed by partial annealing, engineered to yield a fine-grained surface layer over a relatively coarser-grained core.
hypothesis.conditions: Processing and subsequent tests conducted at room temperature on fastener-sized components; testing under standard mechanical and corrosive environments.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: A graded microstructure where the fine surface grains enhance passivation and mechanical strength, while the coarser interior grains reduce the cumulative grain boundary area, thus limiting creep-related deformation.
hypothesis.mechanism: The fine-grained surface layer increases resistance to surface-initiated damage and corrosion by promoting a more uniform and adherent passive oxide film, and increases localized strength via the Hall–Petch effect. Simultaneously, the coarser-grained interior minimizes the propensity for grain-boundary sliding, thereby decreasing room-temperature creep. This duality harnesses both fine and coarse grain advantages.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Overall improvement in fatigue and wear resistance (mechanical durability), lower creep strain under constant load conditions, and a reduced corrosion rate compared to a homogenously grained alloy. The improvement is expected to be modest but significant for aerospace fastener reliability.
hypothesis.baseline: The original as-cast HEA with a uniform grain size distribution that conforms to the inverse Hall–Petch behavior at very fine grain sizes.
hypothesis.boundary: The process must be carefully controlled to avoid over-refinement (which could trigger the inverse Hall–Petch effect) and ensure a proper gradation between surface and core grains. Effects are expected primarily at room temperature and for components where surface condition is critical (e.g., fasteners).
hypothesis.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement and optimum gradient profile are not precisely predictable without further experimental calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two sets of samples: one with a homogeneous grain structure (control) and another processed with the designed thermo-mechanical route to yield a bimodal grain structure. Subject both sets to mechanical tensile tests, constant-load creep tests, and corrosion tests (e.g., salt spray or electrochemical corrosion tests).
measurements: Surface hardness and yield strength
Creep strain under a constant load over time
Corrosion current density and pit formation analysis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the processed, bimodal-grain samples do not outperform the homogeneous grain samples in terms of higher surface hardness, lower creep strain, and improved corrosion metrics, then the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C8

source_paper.title: A Lightweight AlTiVNb High-Entropy Alloy Film with High Strength-Ductility Synergy and Corrosion Resistance.

hypotheses.builds_on: the paper’s observation that the amorphous microstructure contributes to high strength and ductility through shear band and island mechanisms, extending that idea by using controlled thermal processing to introduce beneficial nanostructural twins.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces a post-deposition rapid thermal annealing approach to engineer a dual-phase microstructure (nano-twins within a partially amorphous matrix), a processing intervention not explored in the paper.

hypothesis.hypothesis: A controlled rapid thermal annealing (RTA) post-treatment of the as-deposited amorphous AlTiVNb HEA film can induce a partial nanocrystallization featuring nano-twin boundaries, thereby enhancing the alloy’s mechanical durability, room-temperature creep resistance, and corrosion resistance.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: The as-deposited amorphous AlTiVNb high-entropy alloy film fabricated via magnetron sputtering.
hypothesis.intervention: Apply a short-duration rapid thermal annealing process (for example, heating to around 500°C for 30 seconds under high vacuum) to induce controlled partial nanocrystallization and nano-twin boundary formation within the film.
hypothesis.conditions: Anneal in a high-vacuum atmosphere to prevent oxidation; ensure the processing temperature and dwell time stay below the threshold for full crystallization to preserve a predominantly amorphous matrix; tests to be conducted at room temperature under conditions relevant to aerospace fasteners and in a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution for corrosion evaluation.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: Development of nano-twin boundaries and dispersed nanocrystals embedded in the remaining amorphous matrix.
hypothesis.mechanism: The nano-twin boundaries and fine nanocrystalline regions impede dislocation motion and local shear banding, contributing to enhanced mechanical strength and improved resistance to room-temperature creep. Concurrently, the retained amorphous phase helps sustain a chemically homogeneous and passivated surface beneficial for corrosion resistance.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated baseline, the RTA-treated film should exhibit improved yield strength and reduced creep deformation (an estimated improvement on the order of 15%, though precise data are uncertain) while maintaining or slightly enhancing the corrosion resistance compared to the original amorphous film.
hypothesis.baseline: The as-deposited amorphous AlTiVNb HEA film as characterized in PMC9735962::web::000.
hypothesis.boundary: The positive effects will hold if the RTA process is maintained within a narrow process window; excessive annealing that leads to full crystallization could compromise corrosion resistance and ductility.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvements are uncertain due to the competing effects of induced nanocrystallization versus potential loss of amorphous passivation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of films: one set of as-deposited amorphous films and another set subjected to the proposed RTA treatment. Use TEM to verify the formation of nano-twin boundaries and partial nanocrystallization. Compare mechanical properties via nanoindentation and compression/creep tests, and assess corrosion behavior with Tafel polarization in a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution.
measurements: TEM microstructural analysis to detect nano-twin boundaries and nanocrystalline regions
Nanoindentation for hardness and modulus measurements
Compression tests and long-term creep strain monitoring
Tafel polarization curves for corrosion assessment
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the RTA-treated films do not exhibit the intended nano-twin/nanocrystalline features, or if there is no statistically significant improvement in at least one of the key performance metrics (mechanical durability, creep resistance, or corrosion resistance) compared to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C14

source_paper.title: Effects of Cold Rolling or Precipitation Hardening Treatment on the Microstructure, Mechanical Properties, and Corrosion Resistance of Ti-Rich Metastable Medium-Entropy Alloys.

hypotheses.builds_on: The paper’s emphasis on the crucial role of surface oxide films (as identified in PMC10744552::web::020::3_3_4_xps) combined with principles of grain refinement via severe plastic deformation (TXT::wikipedia::Rolling_(metalworking)::009), extended to tailor surface properties in HEAs.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes a surface-specific, single intervention strategy (SMAT followed by rapid passivation) to engineer a nanocrystalline, ultra-hard surface in aerospace HEAs, targeting improvements in mechanical durability and corrosion resistance at the most critical regions—an approach that diverges from the bulk treatments explored in the referenced paper.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Surface mechanical attrition treatment (SMAT) followed by immediate room-temperature passivation will create a nanocrystalline, ultra-hard surface layer on the aerospace HEA, leading to enhanced mechanical durability at the critical fastener interface, reduced surface-initiated creep and fatigue, and improved corrosion resistance.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: An aerospace HEA in its conventionally processed, finished state with a standard passive oxide layer.
hypothesis.intervention: Apply a high-energy surface mechanical attrition treatment (SMAT) to induce severe plastic deformation in a thin surface layer, immediately followed by natural or assisted room-temperature passivation to re-form an optimized, protective oxide film.
hypothesis.conditions: Ambient conditions mimicking aerospace fastener service, where surface integrity is critical under cyclic mechanical loads and corrosive exposure.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: A nanocrystalline surface layer (on the order of tens of nanometers in thickness) featuring high dislocation density and grain refinement, overlaid by a rapidly re-formed, uniform passive oxide film.
hypothesis.mechanism: SMAT induces a drastic refinement of the surface grains, increasing hardness and resistance to crack initiation and propagation, thereby enhancing mechanical durability and curtailing surface creep (which often initiates failure). The nanostructured surface also offers abundant nucleation sites for a rapid, uniform passivation process, resulting in a more protective, less defective oxide layer against corrosive attack.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated HEA specimens, the SMAT-treated surfaces are expected to show a significant increase in surface hardness (e.g., 30–50% improvement), reduced local creep and fatigue initiation under cyclic loading, and improved corrosion resistance evidenced by higher pitting potentials and lower corrosion current densities in electrochemical tests.
hypothesis.baseline: HEA fasteners with standard surface finish and an as-formed passive oxide layer from conventional processing.
hypothesis.boundary: The intervention’s benefits are limited to the surface and depend on achieving an optimal balance: too aggressive SMAT may lead to excessive roughness or introduce defects that impair passivation, while insufficient treatment may not yield the necessary nanocrystallinity.

hypothesis.baseline: The unmodified AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy with fine lamellar microstructure, as characterized in the provided paper.
hypothesis.boundary: Performance improvements expected under industrial fastener conditions: cyclic temperature fluctuations, sustained mechanical loads (including room-temperature creep), and corrosive environments up to moderate elevated temperatures (but below temperatures where precipitate coarsening or dissolution may occur).
hypothesis.uncertainty: Exact quantitative gains in strength and creep resistance are not fully predictable without experimental calibration; the effect on ductility in the presence of tungsten precipitates is modest but uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one with the standard AlCoCrFeNi2.1 composition and one with an added 0.2 at.% tungsten under identical melting and heat-treatment conditions. Perform tensile tests, creep tests at room and elevated temperatures, and corrosion tests in a simulated corrosive environment.

Creep strain rate under a prescribed constant load
Corrosion rate via electrochemical methods (e.g., potentiodynamic polarization)
Microstructural characterization (TEM/SEM) to confirm nano-precipitate formation

hypotheses.label: C2

source_paper.title: Molten Salt Corrosion Behavior of Dual-Phase High Entropy Alloy for Concentrating Solar Power Systems.

hypotheses.builds_on: findings regarding the selective dissolution of the B2 phase and micro-galvanic interaction in dual-phase AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (see PMC9955357::web::005 and PMC9955357::web::014) combined with principles of refractory metal strengthening.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces a specific alloying addition (Nb) to modify interphase stability and performance, offering a new compositional tuning route not previously reported in the paper.

hypothesis.hypothesis: A minor compositional modification by adding a small quantity of niobium (Nb) can stabilize the B2 phase and reinforce the overall alloy through solid solution strengthening and potential formation of fine Nb-rich precipitates, thus boosting both high-temperature performance and room-temperature creep resistance.

hypothesis.intervention: Introduce 1–2 atomic percent of Nb into the master alloy during vacuum arc melting, ensuring uniform distribution to maintain the eutectic lamellar structure.

hypothesis.mechanism: Nb atoms, being refractory, can strengthen the B2 phase by solid solution hardening and potentially form fine, undissolved precipitates. This reduces the electrochemical potential difference with the FCC phase, thereby diminishing micro-galvanic corrosion and slowing room-temperature creep by enhancing high-temperature stability and load transfer.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Improved yield strength and creep resistance (expected improvements may be modest but measurable), along with reduced selective dissolution of the B2 phase under corrosive molten salt exposure.
hypothesis.baseline: The original AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy with moderate mechanical performance and pronounced selective corrosion of the B2 phase.
hypothesis.boundary: The Nb concentration must remain low (<3 at.%) to avoid formation of coarse intermetallic phases that could embrittle the alloy. The alloying should not disrupt the fine lamellar eutectic structure.
hypothesis.uncertainty: Although Nb is known for strengthening in many alloys, its effect in this specific high-entropy eutectic system and under simultaneous thermal and corrosive stresses has uncertainty in magnitude.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloys with and without 1–2 at.% Nb addition. Perform microstructural characterization (SEM/EDS/EBSD) to confirm phase stability and measure mechanical properties (tensile strength, creep tests at room and elevated temperature) as well as corrosion behavior in molten salt.
measurements: Mechanical testing (yield strength, creep rate)
Corrosion tests (mass loss, electrochemical tests in NaCl-KCl-MgCl2)
Microstructural analyses (phase identification)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Nb-doped alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in strength, creep behavior or corrosion resistance compared to the undoped alloy (e.g., less than 10% improvement), or if the microstructure deteriorates (loss of lamellar morphology), then the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C4

source_paper.title: Phase-Specific Damage Tolerance of a Eutectic High Entropy Alloy.

hypotheses.builds_on: The concept that eutectic microstructure performance can be tuned by processing routes, as noted in the literature and supported by background on eutectic systems and superalloy design.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This approach extends the work by applying directional solidification—a processing intervention not reported in the paper—to tailor the microstructure orientation, thereby addressing the combined demands of extreme temperature fluctuations, load, creep, and corrosion for fastener applications.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Implement directional solidification to align the lamellar phases along the principal loading axis.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: Uniform, fine lamellar AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA produced via conventional vacuum-arc melting and casting.
hypothesis.intervention: Adopt a directional solidification process during casting to induce anisotropy in the lamellar microstructure, aligning the L12 and B2 phases parallel (or at an optimized angle) to the anticipated load direction.
hypothesis.conditions: Use a controlled cooling system with a defined thermal gradient during solidification; operating conditions remain similar to fastener applications (extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term load, room-temperature creep, and corrosive environments).
hypothesis.structural_mediator: Aligned lamellar architecture with optimized phase orientation.
hypothesis.mechanism: Directional solidification will reduce misorientation between the phases, thus lowering stress concentration at phase interfaces when fasteners are subjected to complex, multi-axial loads and thermal cycling. Improved alignment facilitates efficient load-transfer along continuous paths, reducing the likelihood of crack initiation at the brittle B2 phase and enhancing overall ductility and creep resistance.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: The fastener material is expected to exhibit enhanced strength, ductility, and improved creep properties, with a more uniform deformation behavior under long-term and cyclic loads. The directional microstructure should also show improved resistance to corrosion-induced damage through more stable phase boundaries.
hypothesis.baseline: Current as-cast alloys with randomly oriented lamellae exhibiting phase-specific performance limitations (particularly in the B2 phase for bending and creep).
hypothesis.boundary: Benefits are likely most pronounced when the directional alignment matches the primary stress direction in fastener applications; misalignment might negate improvements. The process must be controllable at a production scale.
hypothesis.uncertainty: Quantitative improvement levels are uncertain until directional solidification parameters are optimized; potential trade-offs in isotropy under multi-directional loading must be examined.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two alloy variants: one via conventional casting and one via directional solidification with aligned lamellar microstructure. Machine specimens into fastener shapes and subject them to tensile, bending, and creep tests under controlled thermal cycling and corrosive environments. Compare phase-specific and overall mechanical responses.

Tensile strength and ductility measurements
Creep strain under constant load
Corrosion rate via standard electrochemical tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the directionally solidified (aligned) alloy does not demonstrate statistically significant improvements in strength, ductility, or creep performance compared to the conventionally cast alloy under relevant test conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C10

source_paper.title: Simultaneous Strength-Ductility Enhancement of a Nano-Lamellar AlCoCrFeNi2.1 Eutectic High Entropy Alloy by Cryo-Rolling and Annealing.

hypotheses.builds_on: The hypothesis builds on the paper’s finding that differences in strain partitioning during cryo-rolling lead to heterogeneous microstructures with beneficial back-stress strengthening. It further manipulates the annealing step to accentuate these differences.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This approach introduces a controlled, two-stage annealing treatment—targeting selective phase evolution—to amplify the strain-gradient effects inherent in the hierarchical microstructure, a strategy not investigated in the paper.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Implement a modified two-stage annealing treatment designed to selectively promote full recrystallization in the FCC (L12) lamellae while only enabling recovery (without full recrystallization) in the B2 regions, thereby accentuating inter-phase strain mismatches and enhancing back-stress strengthening.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: Uniform, fine lamellar AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy that has been cryo-rolled to high deformation levels (e.g., 90% thickness reduction) with distinct strain partitioning between FCC and B2 phases.
hypothesis.intervention: Replace the single-step annealing (800 °C for 1 hour) with a two-stage annealing cycle: first, a low-temperature anneal (e.g., 650 °C for 20–30 minutes) to initiate partial recovery in the B2 phase while modestly softening the heavily deformed FCC lamellae; followed by a rapid ramp to 800 °C for a short duration (e.g., 10–15 minutes) to complete recrystallization in the FCC phase.
hypothesis.conditions: Annealing must be performed in an inert atmosphere to prevent oxidation. Process parameters (temperature, time, and heating rate) must be optimized so that the B2 phase only recovers (preserving low dislocation density and LAB structures) while the FCC phase undergoes extensive recrystallization with retained high dislocation density at interfaces.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: A more pronounced contrast in microstructural states between the FCC lamellae (fully recrystallized, ultrafine grains) and the B2 regions (primarily recovered but not recrystallized) that intensifies inter-phase strain gradients and amplifies back-stress effects.
hypothesis.mechanism: The two-stage annealing regimen provides a selective thermal driving force: the initial lower-temperature hold allows the B2 phase, which suffers from lower stored energy due to reduced strain during cryo-rolling, to recover without undergoing full recrystallization. In contrast, the heavily deformed FCC lamellae, with high stored energy, fully recrystallize upon the brief higher-temperature pulse. This deliberate mismatch in microstructural evolution intensifies strain gradients at phase boundaries, enhances pile-up of geometrically necessary dislocations, and thereby results in increased yield strength and improved resistance to creep without sacrificing ductility.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Relative to the standard single-stage annealing, the modified annealing schedule is predicted to yield an alloy with a higher yield strength and enhanced creep resistance (possibly in the 10–20% range) while maintaining comparable or slightly improved ductility, owing to the more effective back‐stress strengthening from steeper inter-phase strain gradients.
hypothesis.baseline: The cryo-rolled and conventionally annealed (800 °C for 1 hour) fine lamellar alloy with its currently achieved hierarchical microstructure.
hypothesis.boundary: The temperature and time of the first annealing stage must be low enough to avoid recrystallization of the B2 phase. The subsequent high-temperature exposure must be brief to prevent overgrowth of grains that would diminish the beneficial microstructural contrast.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The precise thermal parameters needed to achieve the desired selective recovery versus recrystallization remain to be determined, and the magnitude of microstructural contrast enhancement is uncertain without systematic parameter mapping.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of cryo-rolled samples: one to be annealed using the traditional single-stage annealing (800 °C for 1 hour) and the other with the proposed two-stage annealing schedule. Use EBSD and TEM to characterize the microstructural evolution in FCC and B2 regions. Conduct tensile and creep tests to assess mechanical performance differences.
measurements: EBSD/TEM for grain size, boundary type and phase distribution
Tensile tests for yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation
Room-temperature creep tests under constant load
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the two-stage annealed samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in yield strength and creep resistance, or if the microstructural analysis does not show the expected selective recrystallization/recovery contrast, then the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C11

source_paper.title: Nanostructuring with Structural-Compositional Dual Heterogeneities Enhances Strength-Ductility Synergy in Eutectic High Entropy Alloy.

hypotheses.builds_on: The paper’s ideas on harnessing phase heterogeneities for strength–ductility synergy, here extended by employing a surface modification strategy to generate protective, stabilizing phases.
hypotheses.what_is_new: Rather than bulk thermomechanical modifications, this approach utilizes laser surface alloying to incorporate a reactive microalloying element (yttrium) that forms a protective dispersion at the surface, directly targeting issues of high-temperature fluctuations, creep, and corrosion resistance in fastener applications.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Implement a surface laser alloying process to infuse a minor amount of a reactive microalloying element (e.g., yttrium) into the high-entropy alloy surface to form a stable, protective oxide dispersion.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: Uniform, fine lamellar AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA with suboptimal strength and plasticity for fastener applications.
hypothesis.intervention: Conduct a laser surface alloying treatment that introduces a thin layer enriched with yttrium on the fasteners, promoting in situ formation of stable yttrium-aluminide/yttrium oxide dispersions.
hypothesis.conditions: Laser alloying should be carried out under controlled atmospheres to ensure proper Y incorporation; subsequent performance tests under rapid temperature fluctuations (including thermal cycling tests), prolonged mechanical loading with room-temperature creep testing, and exposure to corrosive media (e.g., acidic or saline environments) will be required.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: A modified surface layer where yttrium segregates and reacts with the alloying elements (especially Al) to form finely dispersed, thermally stable Y-rich oxides or intermetallic compounds.
hypothesis.mechanism: Yttrium is known to improve oxidation resistance and suppress grain-boundary weakening by forming adherent, protective oxide scales. The newly formed dispersion strengthens the surface by impeding dislocation motion and enhancing grain boundary cohesion, thus increasing both the high-temperature creep resistance and corrosion resistance. Its beneficial influence on the surface microstructure also contributes to overall load sharing by mitigating surface-initiated failures.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: The laser-alloyed fasteners will exhibit improved surface hardness, enhanced yield strength and creep resistance at the interface under long-term load, and superior corrosion protection, leading to a longer service life under extreme operational conditions relative to the untreated alloy.
hypothesis.baseline: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 fasteners with a uniform lamellar state lacking the additional surface strengthening or corrosion protection provided by reactive element alloying.
hypothesis.boundary: The treatment effect is confined to a surface depth of a few tens of microns; thus, while bulk properties remain governed by the base microstructure, the overall fastener performance in corrosive and high cyclic load environments is improved. Laser parameters must be controlled to prevent excessive dilution or thermal damage.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The precise thickness and uniformity of the modified layer and its long-term thermal stability under extreme cycling need to be validated; the quantitative impact on room-temperature creep is less certain and requires extensive testing.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of fastener specimens using laser surface alloying with a controlled yttrium content and compare with unmodified samples. Characterize the surface microstructure with SEM/TEM/EDS to confirm the presence of Y-rich phases. Perform tensile, creep, thermal cycling, and corrosion tests.
measurements: Surface and cross-sectional microhardness
Phase identification and elemental mapping (SEM/EDS, TEM)
Creep tests under constant load at room temperature
Corrosion rate measurements (electrochemical impedance or salt spray tests)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the laser-alloyed samples do not form a continuous Y-rich dispersion layer or if there is no statistically significant improvement in surface hardness, creep resistance, and corrosion behavior compared with controls, the hypothesis will be considered disproven.

hypotheses.label: C13

source_paper.title: Corrosion Behavior of the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 Eutectic High-Entropy Alloy in Chloride-Containing Sulfuric Acid Solutions at Different Temperatures.

hypotheses.builds_on: The mechanism identified in the paper regarding the role of heterogeneous phase interfaces in corrosion (PMC9319277::web::022) and established precipitation-strengthening principles from superalloy literature.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis extends the paper’s discussion by purposely engineering the lamellar microstructure through a novel aging treatment to induce beneficial nano-precipitates that simultaneously address mechanical deficiencies and reduce detrimental galvanic effects.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Develop a post-solidification aging treatment to promote the precipitation of nanometer-scale intermetallic phases within the lamellar structure, thereby enhancing both strength and creep resistance while reducing galvanic corrosion.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: Uniform, fine lamellar AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy exhibiting distinct B2 and L12 phases with a non-optimized interface that contributes to both mechanical weakness and galvanic corrosion.
hypothesis.intervention: Introduce a controlled sub-critical annealing step followed by artificial aging at an optimized temperature-time schedule to precipitate a uniform dispersion of nano-scale, coherent intermetallic (γ'‑like) particles at lamellar interfaces.
hypothesis.conditions: The heat treatment is applied post-casting and homogenization under an inert atmosphere to prevent oxidation. The treatment parameters are chosen to ensure stability over service conditions ranging from room temperature to moderate elevated temperatures (up to ~60 °C) and under long-term mechanical loading.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: Formation of finely dispersed nano-scale precipitates at phase boundaries that serve as obstacles to dislocation motion and help homogenize the local electrochemical potential differences between the B2 and L12 phases.
hypothesis.mechanism: The controlled aging process encourages the nucleation of nanometric intermetallic precipitates that enhance yield strength by impeding dislocation glide and reducing creep through precipitate strengthening. Additionally, a more chemically and structurally uniform interphase boundary reduces the galvanic effect between the B2 and L12 regions, thereby mitigating localized corrosion initiated by passive film breakdown observed in the paper (PMC9319277::web::021, PMC9319277::web::022).
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Improved yield strength and reduced rate of room-temperature creep, with a concomitant reduction in localized galvanic corrosion; expected improvements may be moderate but decisively beneficial for fastener performance, though precise quantitative gains remain to be established.
hypothesis.baseline: The as-prepared AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA in its uniform, fine lamellar state without any aging treatment, exhibiting weaknesses in both strength and corrosion resistance due to unmodified phase interfaces.
hypothesis.boundary: Effective provided that the aging temperature remains below levels that could coarsen the lamellae or dissolve precipitates, thus maintaining stability in service environments up to ~60 °C and for long-term mechanochemical loading.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The optimal aging parameters (time and temperature) for maximum mechanical and corrosion benefit must be tuned experimentally; the extent of improvement in cyclic loading and corrosive resistance is not precisely predictable.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two sets of alloy samples: one set receives the proposed aging treatment and the other remains in the as-cast state. Characterize the precipitate formation via TEM and XRD, and subject both sets to tensile, creep, and corrosion tests (using potentiodynamic polarization in chloride-containing solutions).
measurements: Precipitate size/distribution (TEM, XRD)
Yield strength and creep strain under defined loads
Corrosion current densities and pitting potentials
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aged samples do not show clear evidence of nano-scale precipitate formation and do not exhibit improvements in mechanical properties (e.g., a significant increase in yield strength or reduced creep rate) along with enhanced corrosion resistance (e.g., higher pitting potential) compared to the as-cast alloy, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C3

source_paper.title: Small-scale mechanical behavior of a eutectic high entropy alloy.

hypotheses.builds_on: The paper’s observation that the lamellar orientation influences deformation and that phase boundaries play a key role in mechanical performance.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces the directional solidification concept to control lamellar orientation, thereby targeting anisotropy and interfacial effects in a manner not addressed in the studied work.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Implement a directional solidification process to preferentially align the lamellae in the loading direction.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: Uniform, fine lamellar AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA produced by conventional casting, with random lamellar orientations.
hypothesis.intervention: Use directional solidification during the casting process so that the eutectic lamellae align parallel to the anticipated load axis of fastener components.
hypothesis.conditions: Solidification under a controlled thermal gradient; operating conditions include extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosive environments typical for fasteners.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: Oriented lamellar interfaces offering increased effective interphase boundary area along the load direction.
hypothesis.mechanism: Aligning the lamellae with the principal load direction reduces stress concentration at the interfaces and enhances load transfer between the ductile L12 and stronger B2 phases. This alignment minimizes deleterious stress states during thermal cycling and reduces creep strain accumulation by distributing deformation more uniformly across the microstructure.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Improved tensile and compressive strength and ductility; reduced anisotropy in mechanical response and potentially moderate improvement in creep resistance, with performance gains of a magnitude that meets industrial standards for fasteners.
hypothesis.baseline: As-cast alloy with randomly oriented lamellae exhibiting tension-compression asymmetry and limited creep resistance.
hypothesis.boundary: Directional solidification parameters must be optimized to retain the fine lamellar spacing; the processing window must avoid formation of coarse colonies.
hypothesis.uncertainty: While directional alignment is known to benefit superalloys (TXT::wikipedia::Superalloy::017), its precise effect on this eutectic alloy's multi-mechanism performance (strength, creep, corrosion) remains to be quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two groups of samples: one using conventional casting and the other via directional solidification. Perform tensile, compressive, creep, and corrosion tests, ensuring testing orientations relative to the loading direction.
measurements: Mechanical strength (tensile and compressive testing)
Creep rate measurements under controlled load
Fractographic analysis to assess failure modes
Microstructural evaluation (EBSD, SEM) to confirm lamella alignment
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the directionally solidified samples do not exhibit improved or more isotropic mechanical properties and creep performance compared to the conventional cast samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C5

source_paper.title: The Exceptional Strong Face-centered Cubic Phase and Semi-coherent Phase Boundary in a Eutectic Dual-phase High Entropy Alloy AlCoCrFeNi.

hypotheses.builds_on: The paper illustrates the role of lamellar structures and phase boundaries in strengthening (PMC6175879::web::004 and PMC6175879::web::011). This hypothesis builds on that by controlling the solidification process to further refine and spatially vary the microstructure.
hypotheses.what_is_new: Instead of adjusting the phase proportions via composition or pre-straining (as discussed in the paper), this proposal introduces the concept of a controlled cooling gradient to engineer a surface gradient in lamellar spacing, a novel processing route for this HEA targeting multi-environment fastener applications.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Refine the lamellar microstructure through directional solidification to create a gradient in lamellar spacing, particularly achieving ultra-fine lamellae near the fastener surface.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: Eutectic dual-phase AlCoCrFeNi2.1 HEA in its uniform, fine lamellar state with spacing around 0.7–1.5 μm.
hypothesis.intervention: Modify the casting process by applying directional solidification with an enhanced cooling rate gradient. The process is adjusted so that the cooling rate is significantly faster near the surface region of the cast, thereby reducing the local lamellar spacing to below ~0.5 μm.
hypothesis.conditions: The revised directional solidification process should be tested in a laboratory scale furnace with a controlled cooling gradient. Operating parameters must ensure that bulk properties are not compromised while the surface microstructure is refined for improved performance in high-stress fastener applications.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: A gradient in the lamellar spacing, where the surface region exhibits an ultra-fine lamellar structure with an increased density of phase boundaries.
hypothesis.mechanism: Finer lamellar spacing increases the overall interphase boundary area, which acts as a stronger obstacle to dislocation motion and provides enhanced impediments to creep deformation. Additionally, a finer microstructure can mitigate thermal expansion mismatches during temperature cycling, thus reducing the initiation of cracks. The increased phase boundary density may also promote rapid strain transfer, improving both strength and damage tolerance.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: An improved combination of strength and ductility in the fastener, with a significant enhancement in resistance to room-temperature creep and superior performance against fatigue induced by extreme temperature fluctuations; expected improvements are moderate but measurable versus the baseline alloy.
hypothesis.baseline: Uniform, fine lamellar structure with typical spacing of 0.7–1.5 μm attained by conventional vacuum arc melting and water-cooled casting.
hypothesis.boundary: This modification is most effective for components where surface performance is critical; improvements might be optimized in fasteners operating within moderate-to-high temperature cycles (up to about 600 °C) and under steady mechanical loads. The bulk alloy properties may remain similar to the baseline.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The degree of improvement depends on the precise control of the cooling gradient. The trade-off between a refined microstructure and possible residual stresses from rapid solidification remains to be quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two sets of HEA fastener samples: one prepared via conventional casting and one via directional solidification with a controlled cooling gradient. Perform microstructural analysis (SEM/TEM) to measure lamellar spacing, then conduct mechanical tests (fatigue, creep, and thermal cycling tests) simulating fastener service conditions.
measurements: Lamellar spacing gradient via microscopy
Tensile and creep tests measuring yield strength and creep rate
Thermal cycling fatigue tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the directionally solidified samples do not show a statistically significant refinement in surface lamellar spacing and corresponding improvements (e.g., >15% better fatigue limit or reduced creep rate) compared to conventionally cast samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C6

source_paper.title: A promising new class of high-temperature alloys: eutectic high-entropy alloys.

hypotheses.builds_on: the principle that the fine eutectic microstructure endows the alloy with enhanced mechanical properties (PMC4145285), extended to the surface via laser processing to exploit dislocation pinning and residual stress benefits.
hypotheses.what_is_new: The proposal of a post-casting surface modification—laser remelting—to create a surface layer with refined microstructure and beneficial compressive stresses, aimed at enhancing performance under the service conditions specific to fasteners.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Apply a post-casting laser surface remelting treatment to induce a refined surface microstructure with compressive residual stresses that enhance mechanical and corrosion performance.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: Bulk-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA with uniform fine lamellar fcc/B2 structure.
hypothesis.intervention: Perform a controlled laser surface remelting process on the as-cast alloy, affecting only a surface layer (~100–200 μm deep).
hypothesis.conditions: Surface treatment conducted in an inert atmosphere or with appropriate shielding; subsequent tests in environments featuring extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosive conditions.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: A modified near-surface microstructure, potentially featuring an even finer eutectic spacing and induced compressive residual stresses.
hypothesis.mechanism: The rapid melting and re-solidification induced by laser remelting creates a refined microstructure at the surface with increased phase boundary density and introduces compressive residual stresses, which can impede crack initiation and propagation. The compressive stresses also counteract tensile stresses under mechanical load and thermal cycling, leading to enhanced creep resistance and improved corrosion behavior by reducing stress corrosion cracking.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Improved fatigue performance, enhanced resistance to creep in the near-surface region, and better corrosion resistance relative to the untreated alloy; the bulk properties remain largely unchanged while the surface properties are significantly optimized.
hypothesis.baseline: As-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy with reported tensile, high-temperature, and creep behaviors (PMC4145285::web::005 and PMC4145285::web::007).
hypothesis.boundary: Effective as long as the laser treatment parameters (energy density, remelt depth) are controlled to avoid inducing undesirable residual stresses or surface cracks. Suitable primarily for fastener components where surface performance is critical.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The depth of the beneficial compressive layer and its uniformity may vary with processing parameters; quantification of long-term creep improvements at the surface under service conditions requires further study.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 fastener components; subject half to laser surface remelting under optimized conditions, leaving the other half untreated. Conduct fatigue, creep (surface-specific indentation creep or micro-creep tests), and corrosion tests (e.g., salt spray and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy).
measurements: Residual stress profiles (via X-ray diffraction)
Surface microstructural characterization (SEM/TEM)
Fatigue life and creep rate measurements on the surface
Corrosion rate and pitting resistance in corrosive media
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If laser-treated samples do not exhibit a measurable compressive stress layer and fail to show enhanced surface fatigue, creep, and corrosion resistance compared to untreated samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C12

source_paper.title: Corrosion Behavior of the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 Eutectic High-Entropy Alloy in Chloride-Containing Sulfuric Acid Solutions at Different Temperatures.

hypotheses.builds_on: The paper’s findings that the native passive film suffers degradation at higher temperatures (PMC9319277::web::012, PMC9319277::web::013) suggest that modifying the surface film could be beneficial.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes using laser nitriding—a process not discussed in the paper—to both improve and stabilize the surface via nitride precipitation and compressive stress, thereby addressing the combined demands of strength, creep resistance, and corrosion performance in fastener applications.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Introduce a laser nitriding surface treatment to form a thin, nitride-strengthened layer on the fastener that enhances both mechanical and corrosion performance.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: Uniform, fine lamellar AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy exhibiting distinct B2 and L12 phases with galvanic coupling and a temperature‐sensitive passive film.
hypothesis.intervention: Apply a localized laser nitriding process that diffuses nitrogen into the top ~10–20 µm of the alloy surface, forming fine nitride precipitates and inducing compressive residual stresses.
hypothesis.conditions: The treatment is conducted on fastener surfaces prior to service. It is designed to be effective through moderate temperature fluctuations (ambient to ~60 °C) and during long-term mechanical loading in corrosive (chloride/sulfuric acid) environments.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: A modified near-surface microstructure with finely dispersed nitrides (e.g., CrN or Fe–N compounds) and compressive residual stresses that reduce dislocation mobility and impede crack initiation.
hypothesis.mechanism: Laser nitriding creates a hardened, compressively stressed surface layer that serves as an artificial barrier against chloride ingress and corrosion while impeding dislocation glide (thus boosting yield strength) and retarding creep-related deformation under long-term load. hypothesis.predicted_outcome: An increase in both surface hardness and yield strength (and hence improved overall fastener performance) as well as a reduction in corrosion current density and pitting frequency relative to the untreated alloy; the magnitude is expected to be significant in applications subject to combined mechanical and corrosive stress, though precise improvement levels are uncertain.
hypothesis.baseline: As-cast and homogenized AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy with a native passive film that deteriorates at higher temperatures.
hypothesis.boundary: Effective in service environments with moderate extreme temperature fluctuations (approximately 5–60 °C) and in corrosive chloride/sulfuric acid conditions; treatment depth is limited to surface phenomena and may not affect bulk creep behavior beyond a certain stress level.
hypothesis.uncertainty: Exact improvement in mechanical property metrics (e.g., yield strength improvement percentage) and long-term stability of the nitrided layer in cyclic temperature conditions require experimental validation.

Yield strength, ductility, and creep strain under defined loads

Corrosion rate measurements (electrochemical tests)
Fatigue and cyclic loading performance comparisons
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nitrided samples do not show significantly reduced corrosion rates, improved surface hardness, and superior resistance to cyclic loading (evidenced by crack initiation and propagation tests) relative to the untreated samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

expert_context.question: Single-phase high-entropy alloys have difficulty achieving a satisfactory strength–ductility balance. Earlier work introduced the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure to enable large-sized production and obtain good strength and plasticity, but its performance still falls short of industrial requirements. Its use in aircraft and spacecraft fasteners further requires stability under extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosion, while relevant creep and corrosion studies remain limited by sample-size and experimental-environment constraints. Given these limitations and design requirements, what single intervention could improve the alloy’s practical performance? Present one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted improvement over the starting material, boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a feasible experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

Creep strain under constant load at elevated temperatures
Corrosion pit density and depth (electrochemical tests)
Microstructural evaluation (precipitate size and distribution)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ti-modified alloy does not show statistically significant improvements in strength, creep resistance, or corrosion performance (or if ductility decreases markedly) compared to the baseline, the hypothesis would be falsified.

Corrosion pit density and depth via microscopy
Mechanical tensile properties post-exposure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated samples do not show statistically significant improvement in creep resistance (i.e., lower steady-state creep rate) and reduced corrosion damage compared to the control group, the hypothesis is falsified.

This enhanced grain‐boundary integrity delays crack initiation under mechanical loading and adverse environmental conditions, which is critical for high-temperature creep and corrosion resistance. hypothesis.predicted_outcome: An improvement in ductility and a reduction in creep and corrosion crack initiation rates are expected – with potential increases in uniform elongation and a modest improvement (perhaps on the order of 10–20%) in long-term performance metrics relative to the PSR alloy without boron.
hypothesis.baseline: The PSR-processed AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy manufactured without any boron addition.
hypothesis.boundary: This benefit is limited to very low boron levels; excess boron could lead to the formation of coarse boride phases that would deteriorate ductility and toughness.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The exact improvement magnitude is uncertain without phase-diagram based thermodynamic and kinetic studies specific to the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 system.

Tensile and creep testing at room and elevated temperatures
Electrochemical corrosion tests (e.g., potentiodynamic polarization)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-added alloy does not show a statistically significant improvement in ductility, reduced creep rate, or enhanced corrosion resistance compared to the control, or if coarse boride phases form and embrittle the material, the hypothesis is falsified.

Electrochemical corrosion tests to assess pitting potential and corrosion current density.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If boron doping does not lead to detectable grain-boundary segregation and the doped alloy does not show improved creep resistance or corrosion performance compared to the undoped baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

Creep strain measured over a fixed duration under a constant load.

hypothesis.baseline: The current as-cast alloy exhibits good strength and ductility but shows limited creep and corrosion resistance under extreme temperature fluctuations.
hypothesis.boundary: Limited to aging treatments that do not induce excessive intermetallic precipitation or significant coarsening of the lamellar structure.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The exact optimal aging parameters and the quantitative extent of property enhancement (e.g., creep rate reduction) remain uncertain until tested.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of alloy samples from the same batch and subject them to varying aging treatments (e.g., different temperatures and times). Perform tensile, creep (at relevant temperatures), and corrosion testing, comparing aged samples to the as-cast baseline.
